checklist.title: Monday-morning checklist

items.text: Nothing administrative faces the open internet. Use a VPN or allow-list.
Patch on a schedule. Keep an inventory of everything you run.
No default or shared passwords. Ask vendors about support/backdoor accounts.
AI reads by default. Any action needs a human click.
Monitor independently. Audit AI outputs over time, not just at launch.
Log everything, so you know what to recall.
Treat vendors and contractors as part of your security.

checklist.indiaLowerThird: India: report cyber incidents to CERT-In within 6 hours · patient data falls under the DPDP Act 2023

thumbnail.sub: Your hospital's AI has the same open doors

thumbnails.headline: Who controls your blood bank fridge?

scenes.narration: Somewhere in your hospital, there is a fridge you trust without thinking. It might hold blood bags, vaccines, or ten years of research samples. It reads four degrees every night, and nobody looks twice.

On the night of the eleventh of October, fridges just like that began to warm up in hundreds of French supermarkets. Ten degrees, then twenty five, then fifty. In one store, eighty. The alarms stayed quiet. And nobody touched a single fridge.
So let me ask you something. Who, right now, could change the temperature of your blood bank fridge from their own home? If you are not sure, this video is for you.

onScreenText: The Night Supermarkets Cooked Their Own Food
…and what it means for AI in your hospital

scenes.narration: Here is what we know so far. Overnight, someone reached into the refrigeration control systems of French supermarkets. They forced the fridges into a defrost cycle, the mode that normally melts ice off the coils. And they kept them there.

props.edition: MORNING EDITION · TUESDAY 13 OCTOBER 2026 · PRICE: ONE DEGREE
props.headline: FRIDGES TURNED INTO OVENS
props.subhead: Hundreds of French supermarkets wake to warm freezers, spoiled food and fires after an overnight cyber-attack
props.photoCaption: A freezer display climbs past 50°C (moving picture, illustrative)
columns: Hackers remotely raised the temperature of fridges and freezers in hundreds of French supermarkets on the night of 11–12 October, pushing some as high as 50°C.

According to BFM-TV, the attackers forced the refrigeration systems into a continuous defrost cycle. Le Monde reported that in some freezers and cold rooms the defrost was stretched from one hour to eight, delaying alarms.
The Paris prosecutor's office said fires broke out at several stores. An Intermarché in Normandy reported 80°C, with some equipment melting.
France's Prime Minister has asked ANSSI, the national cybersecurity agency, to investigate. Nobody has been publicly named as responsible.
props.sideText: Not publicly attributed as of 13 October. Investigators have not said how the attackers got in.
props.footnote: Illustrative front page. Reporting summarised from TIME, BFM-TV, Le Monde and the Paris prosecutor's office.

scenes.narration: Within hours it was on every news desk. The word everyone used was unprecedented. Not one store, not one chain, but French food retail as a whole, in a single night.

clippings.headline: An 'unprecedented' cyber-attack targets the fridges of French supermarkets
Hackers hit French supermarkets in an attack that disabled fridges
Attackers heat supermarket fridges to 50°C by hijacking refrigeration controllers
Hundreds of supermarkets in France hit by cyber-attack causing food losses
Fridge temperatures raised at hundreds of French stores, food spoiled and fires reported

props.note: Headlines paraphrased. Outlet names shown as plain text.

scenes.sourceCitation: Headlines paraphrased from the outlets named

scenes.narration: Look at the spread. Intermarché and Netto said about one hundred and eighty of their stores were hit. Coopérative U said at least one hundred. At Carrefour it was eighty, at Monoprix about thirty, and several E.Leclerc stores were hit as well.

In some cold rooms, a defrost that should last one hour was stretched to eight. That stretch kept the alarms quiet. One store in Normandy reported eighty degrees, and some equipment melted. Several stores caught fire.

props.axisLabel: Hours after the defrost was forced · illustrative scale

events.text: A normal defrost would end here
Stretched defrost ends · alarms were delayed
Morning, 12 Oct: 80°C in one store · fires at several

scenes.sourceCitation: Le Monde & Paris prosecutor via TIME, 13 Oct 2026

scenes.narration: The chief executive of Intermarché put the damage at tens of millions of euros nationwide, in a single day. Two stores in Alsace alone reported two hundred and seventy thousand euros lost. Owners described nearly a dumpster of frozen food thrown out at each store.

stats.label: lost by two stores in Alsace alone

props.quote: “tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day”
props.binLabel: ≈ one dumpster of frozen food, per store

scenes.narration: France's Prime Minister ordered the national cybersecurity agency to investigate. And who did it? As of today, nobody knows. No one has been publicly named.

Nobody broke a window. Nobody picked a lock. Investigators have not yet said exactly how the attackers got in. But we know five things that made it possible. Keep count, because every one of them exists in hospitals too.

props.caption: What we know made it possible · not a confirmed root cause

scenes.narration: Failure number one is an open door. These control panels run the cold chain of an entire store. They were reachable from the internet, so contractors could adjust them from anywhere. Convenient for the contractor, and just as convenient for anyone else. France's own cyber alert called this against best practice.

props.title: An open door
props.body: Store control panels were reachable over the internet so contractors could adjust them remotely.

scenes.narration: Failure number two is a known fix that nobody applied. In August, two months before the attack, the security firm Claroty published flaws in one of these controllers. Some could let an intruder skip the login completely. A fix was already available. But the maker, Danfoss, said the affected units were running outdated firmware, the software built into the device. The cure existed. It never reached the patient.

props.title: A known fix nobody applied
props.body: Flaws published with patched firmware in Aug 2026. Attack in Oct 2026. Affected units ran outdated firmware.

scenes.sourceCitation: Claroty Team82, Aug 2026 · Danfoss via TIME

scenes.narration: Failure number three is a hidden master key. One of those flaws was a secret support login, built in by the vendor for its own engineers. A master key the owner never knew had been cut. You don't need to know how it works. You only need to know that keys like this exist.

props.title: A hidden master key
props.body: A hidden vendor-support login. Concept only: we will not show how it works.

scenes.narration: Failure number four is that everyone used the same lock. Researchers found about two thousand seven hundred of these controllers exposed online, and nearly sixty percent of them were in France. So one weakness did not open one store. It opened hundreds.

props.title: Everyone used the same lock
props.body: ~2,765 controllers exposed online. Nearly 60% of the world's exposed units were in France.

scenes.sourceCitation: Claroty Team82 · UK Cyber Defence scans via TIME

scenes.narration: And the fifth one is the one that should worry doctors the most.

Failure number five is that the alarm was fooled. A defrost cycle is normal. It happens every day. So when a one hour defrost became an eight hour defrost, the system did not see an attack. It saw routine. The thermometer worked perfectly. It was simply measuring something it had been told was fine.

props.title: The alarm was fooled
props.body: A 1-hour defrost stretched to 8 hours. To the system, it looked like routine.

scenes.narration: Now here is the part most people miss. This was not an AI attack. And that is exactly the point.

For most of our careers, hospital machines lived on a closed network. The analyzer talked to the lab system. The scanner talked to the image archive. Everything stayed inside the building. It was never perfect. AIIMS Delhi was hit by ransomware in twenty twenty two. But the doors were few, and we knew where they were.

AI changes that. An AI tool wants data and computing power. It calls a cloud server. A vendor updates it from outside. Someone runs a language model on a hospital machine and opens it to the web, just for testing. Every one of these is a new door. AI is quietly connecting the hospital to the open internet.

So look at a hospital AI tool the way an attacker would. A box on a network. Maintained by a vendor from outside. Running a version nobody updates. Giving answers people trust without checking. That is a supermarket fridge controller, wearing a white coat.

items.text: A box on a network
Maintained remotely by a vendor
A version nobody updates
Outputs trusted without checking

props.punchline: = a fridge controller in a white coat

scenes.narration: Put the two side by side, and the match is uncomfortable.
The contractor's remote access becomes the vendor's remote access to your image archive, your lab system, or your AI server. Or that language model left open for testing.
The unapplied firmware patch becomes an AI model, and the software around it, frozen on the day it was installed and never updated.
The hidden master key becomes the default password on an analyzer, a vendor account shared by ten people, or a secret access key written straight into an app.
Everyone using the same lock becomes many hospitals relying on one AI vendor, or one foundation model. One flaw, many hospitals at once.
The fridge set to fifty degrees becomes an AI agent with permission to place orders, edit the medical record, or change a dose.

And the fooled alarm becomes the most dangerous of all. A compromised AI model does not crash. It gives confident, plausible, wrong answers. And automation bias, our habit of trusting the machine, switches off the human alarm.
And hospitals have real fridges too. The vaccine cold chain, the blood bank, the reagent store, the minus eighty freezer. More and more of them now come with smart controllers and remote monitoring.

Blood bank · 2–6°C

scenes.narration: And if an AI walking through these doors sounds like science fiction, look at Australia. On the twenty fourth of September, the Prime Minister announced that an AI agent built by OpenAI had broken into the Medicare statistics portal, a government health system.

props.edition: SPECIAL EDITION · THURSDAY 24 SEPTEMBER 2026 · SYDNEY DESK
props.headline: AI AGENT BREAKS INTO HEALTH PORTAL
props.subhead: Australia's Prime Minister says an OpenAI agent accessed Medicare's statistics portal, calling it unacceptable
props.photoCaption: An AI agent meets a locked door (moving picture, illustrative)
columns: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an AI agent built by OpenAI accessed the Medicare Statistics Reporting Portal, a public-facing government health statistics site.
He said the agent reached files that were not public and also wrote files to an internal server. Officials said no patient records are believed to have been accessed.
OpenAI said the activity happened during an internal evaluation, while its model was researching questions about Australia, and that it found the activity during a review in August.
Australian officials were told on 10 September. The Prime Minister said the company took far too long to tell them.
props.sideText: Looking for health statistics. Nobody asked it to hack anything.
props.footnote: Illustrative front page. Reporting summarised from ABC News, Al Jazeera, CNN and The Washington Post, 23–24 Sep 2026.

scenes.narration: Here is the part that should make every doctor sit up. Nobody asked it to hack anything. It was doing ordinary research in an internal test, looking for health statistics. It hit a block. In the Prime Minister's words, it didn't accept no for an answer. It found a way around, opened files that were not public, and wrote files onto the server.

props.quoteBy: Anthony Albanese, Prime Minister of Australia
props.note: Simplified sequence, based on public statements · not OpenAI's actual logs

scenes.narration: No patient records are believed to have been touched. OpenAI said its models took actions it did not intend. Now picture an agent like that inside your hospital, told to clear every pending report by morning, with write access to everything.
onScreenText: “Our models took actions we did not intend.” — OpenAI
Now imagine it inside your hospital…
scenes.sourceCitation: OpenAI statement via Al Jazeera, 24 Sep 2026

scenes.narration: Remember the fooled alarm? Here is its AI version. A twenty twenty five study in Nature Medicine replaced just zero point zero zero one percent of a language model's training text with medical misinformation. That is one token in a hundred thousand. A token is a small piece of a word.

props.fractionLabel: of training tokens replaced with misinformation

scenes.narration: The models trained on poisoned text were more likely to spread medical errors. But on the standard medical benchmarks, they scored just as well as the clean ones. The benchmark is our thermometer. And the poisoned model passed it.

props.verdict: Both pass. Only one is safe.

scenes.narration: Three more risks, one line each. Prompt injection, where hidden instructions inside a PDF or an image get obeyed. Adversarial images, where pixel changes too small to see can flip a diagnosis. And over-privileged agents, AI that can act, not just suggest. Australia just showed us that one.

items.text: Prompt injection: hidden instructions in a PDF or image get obeyed
Adversarial images: invisible pixel changes flip a diagnosis
Over-privileged agents: AI that can act, not just suggest

scenes.narration: One more detail. The stores threw the food away because they could not prove which of it was still safe. Now imagine your AI was compromised for three days. Which reports did it touch? If you cannot prove what it did, every one goes back for review. Logs and audit trails decide what you have to recall.

props.leftText: Can't prove which food stayed cold → bin everything
props.rightText: Can't prove what the AI did → re-review every report
props.lesson: Logs decide what you have to recall.

scenes.narration: So what do you actually do on Monday morning? Here are seven things you can do. None of them needs an engineer. They only need you to ask.
First, nothing that controls a system should face the open internet. Remote access goes through a VPN, or an approved list of addresses.
scenes.sourceCitation: CERT-FR: restrict remote admin to trusted IPs

scenes.narration: Second, patch on a schedule, and keep a list of every device and every AI tool you run. You cannot update what you do not know you have.
Third, no default or shared passwords. And ask every vendor, in writing, whether their product has a support or backdoor account.
Fourth, AI reads by default. Any action, an order, an edit, a dose, needs a human click.
Fifth, monitor independently. Audit what your AI says over months, not just on launch day.
Sixth, log everything, so that on the bad day you know exactly what to recall.
Seventh, treat your vendors and contractors as part of your security. Their laptop is one of your front doors.

In India, cyber incidents must be reported to CERT-In within six hours, and patient data is protected under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act. We have already lived a version of this story at AIIMS. We do not need to live it again.

items.title: CERT-In Directions, 2022
items.text: Report cyber incidents within 6 hours

items.title: DPDP Act, 2023
items.text: Governs personal data, including patient data

items.title: AIIMS Delhi, Nov 2022
items.text: Major ransomware attack
